(a) The Board shall take such action as may be appropriate to enforce any right accruing to the United States or any officer or agency thereof as a result of the commitment or issuance of guarantees under this Act. 
    (b) 
If the Corporation undertakes a sale of any asset having a value in excess of $5,000,000, and if the Board determines such sale is likely to impair the ability and capacity of the Corporation to repay the guaranteed loans as scheduled, or to impair the ability of the Corporation to continue as a going concern or to meet such other tests of viability as the Board shall prescribe, the Board shall not issue any further guarantees for loans under this Act, and all guaranteed loans made prior to such determination shall be due and payable in full.
 
    (c) 
If the Corporation enters into any contract, including but not limited to future wage and benefit settlements, having an aggregate value of $10,000,000 or more, the Board shall determine and certify that the performance of the obligations of the Corporation pursuant to such contract will not reduce the ability of the Corporation to repay the guaranteed loans as scheduled, will not conflict with the Corporation’s operating plan or financing plan as required under this Act, and will not impair the ability of the Corporation to continue as a going concern or to meet such other tests of viability as the Board shall prescribe. If in any case such determination and certification cannot be made, the Board shall not issue any further guarantees for loans under this Act until such certification can be made, and all loans guaranteed under this Act shall be due and payable in full.
 
    (d) 
The Board shall be entitled to recover from the borrower, or from any other person liable therefor, the amount of all payments made pursuant to any guarantee entered into under this Act, and upon making any such payment, the Board shall be subrogated to all the rights of the recipient thereof.
 
    (e) 
The remedies provided in this Act shall be cumulative and not in limitation of or substitution for any other remedy available to the Board or the United States.
 
    (f) 
The Board may bring action in any United States district court or any other appropriate court to enforce compliance with the provisions of the Act or any agreement related thereto and such court shall have jurisdiction to enforce such compliance and enter such orders as maybe appropriate.
 
    (g) 
A loan shall not be guaranteed under this Act if the income from such loan is excluded from gross income for purposes of chapter 1 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 or if the guarantee provides significant collateral or security to other obligations, the income from which is so excluded.
 
    (h) 
If any provision of this Act is held to be invalid or the application of such provision to any person or circumstance is held to be invalid by a court of competent jurisdiction, the remainder of this Act, or the application of such provision to persons or circumstances other than those as to which it is held invalid, shall not be affected thereby.
 
    (i)
        (1) Notwithstanding any other provision of law and subject to paragraphs (2), (3), and (4), whenever any person is indebted to the United States as a result of any loan guarantee issued under this Act and such person is insolvent or is a debtor in a case under title 11, United States Code, the debts due to the United States shall be satisfied first. 
        (2) 
Subject to paragraphs (3) and (4), the Board may waive the priority established in paragraph (1) if—

            (A) 
the Board determines that the waiver of such priority is necessary to facilitate the ability of the Corporation or any borrower to obtain financing; and
 
            (B) 
the Board determines that, despite such waiver, there is a reasonable prospect of repayment of the loans guaranteed under this Act.
  
        (3) 
Subject to paragraph (4), waivers under paragraph (2) may only be issued—

            (A) 
with respect to any State or local government;
 
            (B) 
with respect to a supplier of the Corporation, except that no supplier of the Corporation may receive waivers under paragraph (2) with respect to claims of such supplier in an amount of more than $100,000; and
 
            (C) 
with respect to loans made after October 17, 1979, by any creditor of the Corporation up to a total of $400,000,000.
  
        (4) 
A waiver under paragraph (2) with respect to a supplier of the Corporation or any creditor of the Corporation under paragraph (3)(1) may not by its terms subordinate the claims of the United States under this Act to those of any other creditor of the Corporation or of any borrower.
  
    (j) 
The Corporation may not pay any dividend on its common or preferred stock during the period beginning on the date of the enactment of this Act and ending on the date on which loan guarantees issued under this Act are no longer outstanding.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the references to court actions, or to tests of viability the Board "shall prescribe", amount to participation. But the litigation provision lets the federal Board sue to enforce compliance; it does not grant any outside party a right to sue over or object to a federal decision. The rest of the section covers the Board's own determinations, certifications, debt priority, waivers and a dividend ban, with no consultation, hearing, comment period or advisory body involving non-federal actors.
fable.s: The Board may bring action in any United States district court or any other appropriate court to enforce compliance with the provisions of the Act or any agreement related thereto

qwen_block.w: This section outlines the enforcement powers and financial safeguards for a federal Board regarding loan guarantees. It details internal determinations by the Board, recovery of funds from borrowers, and the Board's right to sue in court. There is no requirement for the Board to consult with, coordinate with, or receive input from outside parties (such as the public, states, or independent experts) before making decisions. The interactions described are between the federal government and borrowers/creditors in an enforcement or contractual capacity, not a participatory decision-making capacity.
qwen_block.s: The Board shall take such action as may be appropriate to enforce any right accruing to the United States or any officer or agency thereof as a result of the commitment or issuance of guarantees under this Act.

opus.w: This section covers the federal Loan Guarantee Board's own enforcement powers: suing, getting repaid, and waiving the government's repayment priority. None of these steps requires consulting or coordinating with anyone outside the federal government. The outsiders mentioned (the Corporation, suppliers, creditors, state and local governments) are only the parties these decisions affect, and none gets a right to sue over or object to a Board decision. The power to sue belongs to the Board itself, which is the government.
opus.s: The Board may bring action in any United States district court or any other appropriate court to enforce compliance with the provisions of the Act or any agreement related thereto
opus.b:
1. **Tempting reading:** This section names outsiders (the Corporation, suppliers, creditors, state or local governments) and talks about court actions. Three passages could look like participation:
   - **The Board can sue.** "The Board may bring action in any United States district court" gives the federal Board a right to sue. No outside party gets a right to challenge a federal decision.
   - **Waivers for state or local governments and suppliers.** These outsiders are only the parties whose claims may get a waiver of the government's first-in-line repayment priority. No one consults them before the Board decides.
   - **"Tests of viability as the Board shall prescribe."** This is the Board setting its own criteria. It is not an explicit grant of authority to issue regulations, so the rulemaking point in Example 6 is a weak fit.

2. **Why it fails:** The Board is made up of federal officials, and every decision here stays inside the federal government. No outside party is consulted, and none gets a right to object.

qwen_chat.w: The section describes the Board's authority to enforce rights, determine loan viability, certify contracts, and waive debt priority. These are unilateral administrative or legal actions taken by a federal agency (the Board) regarding financial instruments and legal claims. There is no requirement for the Board to consult, coordinate with, or seek input from outside parties (such as the public, states, or experts) before making these decisions. The interactions with borrowers or creditors are adversarial or contractual, not participatory in the sense defined.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the Board's interactions with borrowers, suppliers, or creditors (e.g., waiving priority, enforcing guarantees) constitute participation because they involve outside parties. However, these are enforcement actions, contractual obligations, or financial transactions, not a process of consulting or coordinating with outside parties *before* making a policy or administrative decision. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits/grants and focuses on consultation/coordination/advisory roles. The Board's actions here are unilateral determinations or legal enforcements, not collaborative decision-making with outsiders.
